brief.head: Advanced, persistent
brief.text: Attacks that are both skilled and sustained point to a state, Ajay Shah said. Private criminals “launch one crime and then they’ll lose interest”. {084-C04}

brief.head: Fight it anyway
brief.text: Most misinformation is homegrown, Amit Varma guessed. Since attribution is hard, fight it wherever it comes from: China, Russia or “some guy sitting in UP”. {084-C13}

brief.head: Debugged in India
brief.text: Global attack groups test their newest zero-day exploits on Indian targets, Ajay Shah said, because breaches here get hushed up. A week later, they hit Europe and America. {084-C12}

brief.head: Sincere, not bought
brief.text: Most pro-Russian views in America are sincerely held, Amit Varma said. Calling them foreign-sponsored is like the Indian government branding dissidents “anti-national”. {084-C14}

brief.head: Lawyers for the CIA
brief.text: Authoritarian states launch dirty tricks easily, Ajay Shah said, free of legislatures and information laws. The CIA, by contrast, has to consult lawyers at every step. {084-C05}

thought.text: We are a linear combination of our influences.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, conceding that Amit Varma had reshaped his way of telling stories

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on hybrid warfare
lead.head: Not quite war, not quite peace
body: Amit Varma began by declaring that he and Ajay Shah are men of peace. They then spent nearly an hour and a half on war, of a kind that often does not look like war at all.
There used to be a simple choice, Shah said: a country was either at peace or at war. Now the world is shaded grey.

At one extreme is explicit war, as between Russia and Ukraine. At the other is explicit peace, as between Japan and the United States. In the middle lies a grey zone of hostile acts. That is the zone of hybrid war.
## Below the threshold
The field’s terms are detection, attribution and response. The ideal attack is one the victim never notices; the next best, one it cannot pin on anyone. Either way, hitting back becomes hard.
“Show me a hostile action that can stay below the attribution threshold,” Shah said. “Okay, that’s the game.” {084-C01}
There is a catch, and it is time. Detection and attribution usually arrive in the end, so the attacker who plays short gets a punch in now and the bill later.

Shah’s toolkit has four drawers: cyber attacks routed through friendly countries’ IP addresses; proxies such as the Wagner group and Lashkar-e-Taiba; information warfare, newly potent on social media; and deniable violence, such as a tanker’s anchor dragged across the Baltic seabed. {084-C03}
## Cheap shots
Hybrid warfare, Shah argued, is the strategy of the weak. Putin, “a very weak player” holding a GDP he put at the size of Italy’s, gets outsized returns from cheap operations.
Every small attack carries a veiled threat of bigger ones, he said, and the fear it breeds strengthens those in the target country who want to make peace.

Yet he would not call it a winning strategy. Pakistan’s hawks might score the 2008 Mumbai attack a success, but the country paid with isolation. It suits, he said, those “managing the headlines and not the country”.

Varma pushed back on how much could be pinned on foreign plots. India’s Hindu-Muslim tensions are homegrown, he said. Shah agreed: information warfare cannot invent a society’s fault lines, only inflame the ones it finds.
## Wake-up call

The most dangerous idea, Shah said, is that all this happens elsewhere, in the Baltic or in Australian elections. By one estimate, about 43 per cent of Russia’s influence campaign on the Ukraine war was conducted in India. {#fortythree}
India should not read the foreign press and conclude that it is safe, he said. It is already part of the global game.

His remedies ran from a faster armed response to terror to better government software. Against information warfare, he argued, the only real defence is a society’s ability to establish what is true: universities, statistics, researchers, trusted media and believable government bodies. {084-C15}
Fact-checkers, Shah said, are “but a thin layer on a deeper societal capability”. And “it is difficult and dangerous to be a truth teller in India today”.

Varma ended with a confession. Every time he visits Shah’s home, he said, he is plied with fruit, biryani and sweets: hybrid warfare, he now realised. “You’re killing me softly with your sugar.” {084-J06}

second.label: The Baltic Sea
second.head: Oops, said the tanker
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a Chinese tanker, a torn seabed and a Finnish boarding party
body: Russia runs a “shadow fleet” of tankers that carry its crude oil to friendly buyers, China and India among them. A Chinese tanker in that fleet, Ajay Shah said, dragged its anchor along the floor of the Baltic Sea, tearing through gas pipelines, oil pipelines and fibre-optic lines. {084-S02}

Even when caught, such a crew can call it an accident. This time the Finnish Navy boarded the ship and detained the crew for interrogation. Shah likened it to India taking Kasab alive in 2008, and called the incident an unprecedented escalation.
Amit Varma imagined the boarding party’s reply to the captain: “We are Finnish, you are finished.” {084-J02}

quote.text: The tanker throws up its hands and says, oops, this was a mistake.

second.caption: the Baltic anchor drag

third.head: Centrifuges in a spin
body: The Israelis, long keen to disrupt Iran’s nuclear programme, got into the operating system of the industrial controllers that ran Iran’s centrifuges, Ajay Shah said. {084-S01}

The code knew the frequencies the machines needed. Whenever scientists asked a centrifuge to do the right thing, it made the centrifuge do the wrong thing. Machines fell apart, and the uranium purification went wrong.
“For a long time the scientists thought that we have not yet solved our R and D problems,” Shah said, “while actually there was clever code that was disrupting them.”

Even after the sabotage was found, Iran was left asking who did it and how to respond. That, Shah said, is the craft of hybrid warfare: staying below the thresholds of detection and attribution. {084-C01}
third.caption: the code in Iran’s centrifuges

p2.title: The grey zone
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s map of hybrid warfare, part by part, and where Amit Varma pushed back

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Four tools, no fingerprints
sections.caption: the hybrid toolkit
body: Imagine India’s electricity grid misbehaving: frequencies going wrong, equipment damaged, and nobody knowing why. That, Ajay Shah said, is a cyber attack still below the detection threshold. {084-C03}

Attribution is no easier. Attackers first log in through a friendly country, so hundreds of IP addresses from Japan may seem to be attacking Indian power systems. Investigators must study the code itself, its DNA and antecedents, and work out which modification happened where.
Russia and China, he said, also grew private cyber gangs on purpose. Caught out, a government can apologise for “some criminals” and offer to jail them.
## Proxies and propaganda

Proxies serve the same end. Wagner let Russia call its fighters mercenaries, and Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed let Pakistan’s government plead “Who me?”. In Donetsk, many local “rebels” were Russian soldiers in guerrilla uniforms.

Propaganda is old, Shah said: the Soviet Union did it, and the West had Voice of America. What is new is social media, whose rabbit holes radicalise and tribalise. He described blow-by-blow evidence that Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Internet Research Agency in St Petersburg stoked American anger all the way to a physical rally in Colorado. {084-S10}
~ Amit Varma accepted that Russia had tried to interfere in the 2016 election, but said its effect was vastly overstated and had no impact on the result. {#overstated}

quote.text: So people have applied themselves to saying what things can I do to harm my enemies without getting to detection or attribution.

sections.label: The incentives
sections.head: The weakling’s weapon
sections.caption: the strategy of the weak
body: Hybrid warfare is chosen because it is optimal for some people, Ajay Shah said. They are “playing their chess game as well as they can”, and it is the strategy of the weak. {084-C02}

Russia, he said, is believed to have tested the idea on Paris: some fourteen fibre-optic cables into the city were cut at once, by people who understood the whole network. It was a nuisance in peacetime. The unstated message was that the same might be done to twenty European cities. {084-S03}
Such fear feeds the peacemakers. Germany’s long softness on Putin, Shah argued, was born of it. Influence operations, he added, are “all very low cost affairs”.
## Late is too late

Deniability need not last forever. In Crimea, Putin’s men in plain clothes, nicknamed the Little Green Men, claimed to be a local militia. The Obama team was fooled for a while, and by the time it understood, the Russian army controlled Crimea. {084-S04}

Democracies are exposed in another way. Divide a country against itself, Shah said, and it cannot mount an effective foreign policy. {084-C07} He called the rise of pro-Russian views in American politics one of Putin’s greatest achievements.
~ Amit Varma replied that Putin invaded no one in Trump’s first term.

quote.text: Hiding inside every small attack is a veiled threat about bigger attacks in the future.

sections.label: The pushback
sections.head: Don’t read history backwards
sections.caption: the hindsight teleology trap
body: Five people inside Pakistan’s ISI, Ajay Shah said, could write a one-sided report card on the 2008 Mumbai attack and high-five all round. But the country paid with isolation as Fortune 500 boards backed away. Such tactics suit those whose “decision horizon is one week”. {084-C09}

Amit Varma pushed back on the examples. The communal strain has run through Indian society all along, he said, as Akshaya Mukul’s history of the Gita Press shows. Foreign powers might act at the margins. {084-R03}

Nor could anyone have planned what followed 26/11. The economy’s slide after P. Chidambaram was moved from the finance ministry, described in Puja Mehra’s *The Lost Decade*, was beyond any plotter. Reading such chains backwards is, Varma said, the “hindsight teleological mistake”. {084-C08}
## Fires, not matches

Shah agreed. The problems are homegrown, he said, but information warfare finds a country’s weak spots and plays on them. Karl Popper, he noted, warned against complex conspiracy theories: nobody can plan so much, “least of all a secret small cabal of conspirators”. {084-J14}
Varma also defended the marketplace of ideas: most pro-Russian views in America, he argued, are sincere, not bought.
~ Shah’s own example of unintended consequences: who could have predicted that the October 7 attack would lead to the fall of the Assad regime?

quote.text: It is deeply totalitarian to say that my view is right, and any other view is some foreign agents are doing it.

sections.label: The spy game
sections.head: Spies, lies and timing
sections.caption: intelligence, early and deep
body: Early detection and attribution are key against information warfare, Ajay Shah said. Once a campaign is exposed, people discount it, because “the people are reasonably bright”. {084-C10}

Amit Varma raised the hard part. Every intelligence agency, including France’s, believed Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, and all of them were wrong. In a sea of noise, how does anyone know what to trust?
Shah answered with three stories. In Iraq, Western agencies trusted documents written by officials too frightened to report failure. In Crimea, they worked out too late what was happening.
## The one that worked

The third was a triumph. In February 2022, before Russia invaded Ukraine, the Biden team published its intelligence: the plan, the dates, which tank would move where. Nobody could then pass the invasion off as a local uprising. {084-S05}

Varma asked about private actors, from a billionaire shorting stocks to “some kid in a pajama in a bedroom”. Shah offered a term of art: APT, or advanced persistent threat. Teenage hackers are rarely advanced, and criminals rarely persist. Only states are both. {084-C04}
~ The footprint of intelligence, Shah said, must widen beyond traditional war to every piece of hybrid warfare, though mistakes will always be made.

quote.text: But if a campaign is detected early and the attribution is done early, then actually the people are reasonably bright.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: The battlefield at home
sections.caption: India as a battlefield
body: The most dangerous thing, Ajay Shah said, is to read about the Baltic Sea or Australian elections and assume nothing is happening in India. His XKDR Forum has a working paper gathering evidence on foreign actors around Indian elections. {084-R02}

In 2021, he said, Meta documented a Russian influence operation in India against the AstraZeneca vaccine. Developed with Oxford and made at scale by the Serum Institute with help from the Gates Foundation, it had helped the subcontinent fight COVID. Russia did not want that goodwill going to the West. {084-S11}
Amit Varma had three shots of it, and was glad. Without the vaccine, he told Shah, “You could have been talking to an empty chair.” Shah’s reply: “Everything is nothing.” {084-J05}
## Records of the powerful

Attacks on India’s power system in 2022 are believed to have come from China, Shah said. So is the hack of AIIMS, which stole the medical records of powerful Indians, “a gold mine” for future covert operations.
~ It is time to wake up, he said, though not to start shouting “foreign hand” at every dissident.

quote.text: Because they did not want Indian goodwill in favor of Oxford University and AstraZeneca, a Western Corporation, and the Gates Foundation.

sections.label: The remedies
sections.head: Guns faster, truth deeper
sections.caption: the defences that work
body: Each threat needs its own answer, Ajay Shah said. Against proxies and terror, build kinetic capability: when the next attack comes at the Taj, “get guns there faster”.

Against cyber attacks, build better systems. India calls itself an IT superpower, yet global attack groups use it as a training ground, he said: misconfigured systems abound, and companies hush up breaches rather than alert vendors. New zero-day attacks are debugged on Indian targets, then taken to Europe and America a week later. {084-C12}
## Truth as a defence

Information warfare demands something deeper. Every society, Shah said, needs epistemic institutions to separate truth from lies: universities, statistics, researchers, trusted media and government bodies that people believe. {084-C15}
Where those institutions are weak, as he said they are in India, manipulators domestic and foreign have a field day.

Amit Varma explained to listeners that epistemic means knowledge. He had earlier argued that misinformation should be fought wherever it comes from, guessing that ninety per cent of it is locally generated. {#ninety}
~ The United States came through Cold War propaganda, Shah said, because trusted people spoke up, wrote and criticised, and were believed.

quote.text: The only way to fight information war is to grow the depth and capability and activism of that epistemic institutional capability.

side.boxText: Detection: does the victim even know it was attacked? Attribution: can it tell who did it? Response: can it hit back? Hybrid warfare, Ajay Shah said, is the craft of staying below the first two thresholds. {084-C01}

contQuote.text: The problems are homegrown. But it is the nature of information warfare that you will identify the difficulties of the country and pour oxygen on the fires.

p3.title: Dispatches from the shadows
p3.deck: A loudspeaker duel, a brave constable, phantom weapons and a buggy study

stories.start: I now want to turn to information warfare and give you an example
stories.end: information matters. You can take morale up, you can take morale down
stories.caption: the Nathu La loudspeakers
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a propaganda war at Nathu La, 1967
stories.head: Loud, clear and incomprehensible
body: In 1965, Amit Varma said, the Indian Army expected China to push into Sikkim through two passes, Jelep La and Nathu La. It ordered a pullback, so they could be defended from wider positions. The general at Jelep La withdrew. Sagat Singh, at Nathu La, refused. {084-S08}

Singh’s thinking, as Varma put it: “What if they just want to occupy?” High ground lets a few men defend against many below. The puzzled Chinese held off, and when fighting came in 1967, at Nathu La and Cho La, they were repelled.

It was at Nathu La, Varma said, drawing on Probal Dasgupta’s *Watershed 1967*, that the Chinese army tried propaganda. It translated its messages into Shuddh Hindi and played them to the Indian soldiers over loudspeakers. {084-S09}

“Now, as you and I and every Indian knows, no one in India speaks Shuddh Hindi,” Varma said. It is an artificial register, born of a 19th-century movement to split Hindustani. And the soldiers were Jats, who had no idea what was being said.
Assuming the broadcasts were working, the Chinese went from four loudspeakers to twelve. {#loudspeakers}

The Indians, bizarrely, had loudspeakers of their own, and shouted propaganda back in Chinese. Ajay Shah asked listeners to spare a thought for those soldiers, working “pre-Google Translate”. {084-J03}
~ Whether India’s Chinese slogans worked, nobody on this side knows. “It’s almost like a comic book thing,” Varma said. Even then, armies understood that information can take morale up or down.
stories.why: Information has always been a weapon of morale, but it works only on an audience that understands it. Get the language wrong and you can scale up a useless operation with complete confidence.
stories.postscript: Varma argued that a Chinese hold on Nathu La could have cut India off from East Pakistan in the 1971 war.

stories.start: Many people forget, but I think one of our great heroes
stories.end: had he died, had all the men died, they had complete plausible deniability
stories.caption: Tukaram Omble
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a constable’s sacrifice in 2008
stories.head: The man who would not let go
body: During the 2008 attack on Mumbai, Amit Varma said, the constable Tukaram Omble was on Marine Drive when Ajmal Kasab, one of the attackers, tried to get away.
Omble grappled and fought with him, and held on so that Kasab could be taken alive. He was shot in the process and died. {084-S06}

Because Kasab survived, India could learn where he was born and trained, and show that this was proxy warfare by Pakistan. “Had all the men died,” Varma said, “they had complete plausible deniability.” {#deniability}
~ Varma accused Ajay Shah of having stolen this talking point earlier, when Shah explained why the Finnish Navy’s boarding of a Chinese tanker in the Baltic mattered so much.
stories.why: In deniable warfare, attribution can hang on a single thread. One constable’s grip turned an anonymous strike into a documented, state-backed operation. Varma called him one of India’s great heroes.

stories.start: we now know why the WMD stuff went wrong in Iraq
stories.end: it doesn't mean you should start cheering that wow, the problem is solved
stories.caption: fake reports from Saddam’s Iraq
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why every intelligence agency got Iraq wrong
stories.head: The weapons that lived on paper
body: Every intelligence agency, Amit Varma noted, even that of France, which opposed the invasion of Iraq, believed Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction. Ajay Shah explained what went wrong.

Under a tyrant who would destroy anyone reporting failure, Iraqi civil servants wrote that they were making great progress. Their biological weapons, the files said, were killing mice; monkeys were next. {084-S12}
Those documents leaked to Western agencies, which believed the hard paper. Saddam refused inspections, and only when an army went in did anyone find the labs empty.

~ “It is Swachh Bharat all over again,” Shah said: nonsense flows up a bureaucracy until the top believes it. A document saying so many toilets were built, he warned, is no reason to start cheering. {084-J13}

quote.text: In Saddam Hussein’s regime, you needed to have that sociological understanding of the Saddam regime, that officials lie to each other.

stories.start: While I'm on the subject, I shall digress and tell the world's best story
stories.end: there were mistakes in the programming, so the result was actually wrong
stories.caption: the short bet that wasn’t
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s “world’s best story”, for researchers
stories.head: A bug in the conspiracy
body: Ajay Shah billed it as the world’s best story, for researchers. Amit Varma said he was “so excited now”, since that sounded like his own habit. {084-J04}

Shortly after the October 7 attack, Shah said, a research paper in America claimed someone had taken a vast short position on Israeli markets just before it. The plotters, it implied, had made half a billion dollars off their own atrocity. {#shortbet}
Then came the punchline. “It turned out that there were mistakes in the programming,” Shah said, “so the result was actually wrong.” {084-S13}
~ Varma, for his part, had already said that the sheer evil of the attack dwarfed any trading profit: “You’re killing eleven hundred people or you’re shorting something?”
stories.why: Terror and profit can mix in principle, which makes attribution harder still. But a sensational finding deserves suspicion until its code has been checked, a lesson Shah aimed squarely at researchers.

quiz.q: What nickname was given to the plain-clothes men who took over Crimea?
quiz.a: The Little Green Men, who claimed to be a local militia, not Russian soldiers.

quiz.q: What does APT stand for, and why does it usually point to a state?
quiz.a: Advanced persistent threat; only states buy such skill and keep at it.

quiz.q: Which constable held Ajmal Kasab on Marine Drive so he could be taken alive?
quiz.a: Tukaram Omble, who was shot and killed keeping Kasab from escaping.

quiz.q: Why did the Chinese loudspeaker propaganda at Nathu La fail with the Jat soldiers?
quiz.a: It was in Shuddh Hindi, an artificial register that nobody in India speaks.

quiz.q: What did the Biden team do with its intelligence before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022?
quiz.a: It made it public: the invasion plan, the dates, which tanks would move where.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did Western agencies believe Iraq had weapons of mass destruction?
quiz.a: Frightened Iraqi officials faked progress reports, and leaked documents were taken at face value.
